Do you have any suggestions for bipods, monopods, or glass?

Bipods — Harris bipod with segmented legs and cant. LaRue tactical Harris bipod combos are rugged and QD for anything with a stud or Picatinny and they carry all sorts of mounting options. You get what you pay for.

Monopods — I’m not a fan forward or aft, and prefer a larger hand held sand bag adjusted to accommodate all manner of stocks. Caldwell makes a great variety, but understand the conditions you will be shooting under and choose the outer material wisely, which is usually some sort of heavy canvas but can also be leather or poly composite, and some come with a rubber padding. There are all kinds, but I tend towards cylindrical, canvas, and medium weight, about 1-1.5 pounds.

Glass — Can o’ worms. Budget rules the day, but the best glass for the money and warranty right now is Vortex. Leupold comes a close second, but the reticle and feature options are limited in the same price category as Vortex, if we are talking $500 and below especially for magnified variable. Above that, you get into high power scopes which for me get into 16x range and $700-800. At $1k and above, you need to do your homework because many of the industry players begin here and top out at around $1500. $1500 and above are where the elite manufacturers live, but Vortex, Bushnell, and Leupold all have their premium offerings well into the $2k range. At $2-2.5 you can get basically whatever feature you want at whatever magnification you want. Believe it or not there are a handful of players that get into the $4-$6k range but you’ll know who they are once you get into that arena. For perspective, I run exclusively Vortex and Leupold for variable scopes, and have lusted after Schmidt and Bender and Nightforce but realize I don’t need them the same way a commuter doesn’t need a Ferrari, but it’d still be nice to drive every once in a while. Also, if you’re gonna get glass, make sure your mounts do them justice. Seekins make great serialized mounts, LaRue makes great QD mounts, but most of the scope manufacturers are going to make a decent set of mounts for their optics. What I wouldn’t recommend is going cheap with a mount because it will tell it’s value over time. Lastly, torque everything to spec, which means get a decent digital torque wrench. The specs aren’t usually astronomical, on the order of 20ft/lbs or so, but it’s a goddamn shame if you go to the range, zero your glass and rifle only to come home and find out the scope is sliding to and fro for lack of certainty...ask me how I know:)
